Speaker B: Why? How about I feel good without any shoulds about it? That you would naturally prefer to feel good, and so you feel good. But if you say you should feel good.

Speaker A: But yeah, like changing your thoughts is easy, but changing your emotions takes some time. It can happen really quickly, but I feel like sometimes then there's a disconnect.

Speaker B: Exactly. But if you don't change your language, if you don't change your thoughts, then you won't change your feelings. But if you continue to have a new avenue of thought, if you continue to gladden the mind and brighten the mind, pretty soon the feelings will go along with that. The feeling of Sukkha, the feeling of I'm not afraid, I feel safe and secure. Why? Because I'm not giving myself thoughts that cause me to be afraid. If I have thoughts of comfort, I can begin to feel comfortable. If I have thoughts of well-being, then I will eventually have the feeling of well-being. And if I have thoughts of being satisfied, I'll begin to feel satisfied. And if I feel like this is a pile of crap, I'll begin to feel like a pile of crap.

Speaker A: So how do you handle the in-between? Like, do you just— oh, you just say like, oh, I'm just gonna take it easy and in a little bit I'll feel good again because I'm being wholesome, or— right.

Speaker B: And then that old rule come up, get off your ass and go do something. Can you see that old rule come up and say, you ought to go do this, you ought to go do that, and rather than, okay, I can do that happily.

Speaker A: Yes, I can do that.

Speaker B: All right, so Callum, what do you think?

Speaker C: Yeah, um, I'd like to ask, because you talked about the right attitude in terms of, um, the concept of self is not to cling to I, me, or mine. What's the correct attitude to have in terms of volition, the attitude towards volition? Because it seems evident to me that it's quite a nebulous concept. You can think about it and talk about it for ages, but you can't ever really pin it down. The cause of volition, the source of volition. So what's the right attitude to have?

Speaker B: Right. Actually, the word volition is often associated with will. Like free will. All right, and the important point is, is that the big argument between is there free will and is there no free will is misguided because of the problem with the definition of the terms. But basically, what if we can define what destiny is, then we can understand the not free will part. All right, so what is destiny is that our thoughts over and over again lead to our feelings, and our feelings over and over again lead to our speech, and our speech over and over again leads to our actions, and our actions over and over again begin to lead to our habits, and our habits over and over again lead to our destiny. And most people get so stuck in their habits that they can't control their destiny, and therefore they are stuck and they've got no free will. But within the concept of the teaching of the Buddha, when we can begin to change our thoughts— because thoughts are easy enough to change if you remember to change them. I mean, hot dog, you change your thoughts 100 times a day without even thinking about it, so it must be pretty easy to do. So all we have to do is start practicing to have some good wholesome thoughts, and then we'll have some good wholesome feelings, and then we'll have some good wholesome speech and good wholesome actions, which will lead then to some new habits. And then that means that the destiny is changing. So we begin to start, we start off in childhood with piling up a destiny. What do you want to do when you grow up? What do you want to do? What's your favorite color? What's your favorite food? Have you ever heard those kinds of questions? Those lead to your destiny. You're destined to love blue because you said it one time when somebody asked you. You're not supposed to change your destiny from, "I liked blue one time, but now I like green," especially when money is the right color. You know, but, "Oh, I'm supposed to like blue," or, "I'm supposed to be a fireman because somebody asked me when I was 4 years old, 'What do you want to be?' and you said fireman. Now you've got a destiny to be a fireman." Well, when we grow up and get into the Dhamma, We can recognize we can change our thought patterns, and by doing that, ultimately we can change our destiny. Destinies would be something like, "He who lives by the sword dies by the sword." And so that young buck who can wield that sword and kill all kinds of people, by the time he's 80 years old, he's been sliced in half a half a dozen times because the younger bucks got him. Someday he needs to put that sword down and change his destiny. If he keeps that sword, he's going to get killed with one. So we have to put those swords down, and then we don't die by the sword. That's the destiny part, is that you can change your destiny. But ultimately, your will is never free. Then in fact, getting your will back and taking it away from destiny takes a lot of right effort, over and over and over and over again, changing each thought one at a time until you do change your habits of thinking. Right? So that leads to the punchline of the joke that I've been building up, that there is no such thing as free will, but there is certainly a thing called expensive will, Are you willing to pay the price to gain your will back? Because will is expensive. You have to put in the right effort to get it. But you see, the philosophers and the Christians and the atheists, they don't go to that kind of detail. They just argue whether there's free will or not.

Speaker A: I gotta go, guys. All right, very much for this call. I really enjoyed this.

Speaker B: Bye-bye. Okay, Daniel, we'll see you later.

### Summary

Based on this Dhamma talk with Dhammarato and Sangha friends, the core themes and advice can be summarized as follows:

### **Central Theme: Freedom Through Present-Moment Investigation, Not Rigid Rules**
The talk consistently warns against creating strict, long-term rules of renunciation (e.g., "I will never use my cell phone again" or "I'm on a diet"). Such rules set you up for failure and create internal conflict. Instead, the path is **moment-to-moment investigation and wise choice**.

### **Key Practical Teachings:**

1.  **The Method Over the Path:** The Noble Eightfold Path is framed not as a distant road, but as a **present-moment method**: **Wake up (mindfulness), look at what's happening (investigation), make a wise change (right effort), and congratulate yourself (gladdening the mind).** This cycle builds confidence and breaks the habit of being a victim to your impulses.

2.  **Dealing with Distractions & Low Motivation:** Don't fight habits with willpower. Instead, maintain a gentle, mindful awareness ("keep one eye on the Dhamma") while engaging in them. By observing the discontent they create, **dispassion (nibbida) arises naturally**, and the mind will naturally turn back to what is wholesome. The Sangha's role is to provide an environment that makes this easier.

3.  **Demystifying Core Concepts:**
    *   **No-Self (Anatta):** Don't get lost in philosophical debate. The practical teaching is **"don't take things personally."** The problem is **selfishness** and clinging to "I, me, mine," not proving or disproving a self.
    *   **Free Will vs. Destiny:** The debate is misguided. We are conditioned by past habits (destiny), but we have **"expensive will"**—we can reclaim agency through the diligent, repeated effort of changing our thoughts in the present moment, which eventually changes our habits and destiny.
    *   **Nibbana:** It is not a magical, otherworldly state. It means **"to cool."** It's the feeling of relaxation, peace, and the ending of the "friction" of craving. It's available now by letting the mind cool off from its demands.
    *   **Enlightenment:** It's twofold: **"to illuminate"** (see things clearly) and **"to lighten"** (drop your burden). It's the practical result of the method, not a magical attainment.

4.  **Overcoming Disempowering Beliefs:** In response to teachings that say "there's nothing to do" (like some Neo-Advaita), the correct attitude is one of **relief and empowerment**. You have the **"3 Ps"**:
    *   **Permission** to feel good without needing external approval.
    *   **Power** to change your thoughts and state.
    *   **Protection**—feeling good won't cause things to fall apart.

5.  **Duality vs. Non-Duality:** Duality arises from wanting, judging (good/bad), and clinging to personal rules. **Unity or "at-one-ment"** is found in the present moment when wanting ceases, and you are in harmony with things as they are. It's like an orchestra tuning to the same note to create harmony instead of noise.

6.  **Meaning and Rules:** All meaning is created by desire. We all carry a "bag of rules," but the content (personal, religious, social) causes separation. The practice is to lighten this bag. The only essential guideline is the Buddha's: **Investigate what causes suffering (dukkha) and abandon it; cultivate what leads to its cessation (nirodha).**

### **Overall Tone & Approach:**
The teaching is **pragmatic, non-dogmatic, and immediate.** It emphasizes:
*   **Simplicity** over complex philosophy.
*   **Present-moment choice** over grand renunciations.
*   **Personal investigation and responsibility** over blind adherence to rules.
*   **A gentle, observational approach** to bad habits rather than violent suppression.

The ultimate goal is portrayed as accessible: **opening the "door to paradise" that is already here by using the method of mindful investigation in the now.**

### Metaphors and Stories

Based on the transcript, the talk uses several core metaphors and illustrative stories to explain Buddhist-inspired concepts about practice, mindset, and freedom. Here’s a breakdown:

### **Key Metaphors and Stories**

**1. The Cell Phone / Media Diet**
   * **Metaphor:** The cell phone (and platforms like YouTube) represents distracting, desire-driven content that can lead to dissatisfaction (*dukkha*).
   * **Lesson:** Instead of making rigid rules ("renunciation") like "I'll never use my phone," the skill is to **mindfully notice** when content makes you unhappy and **change the subject**—switch to something wholesome (e.g., "go back to Skype and see some happy people"). This illustrates mindful choice over rigid prohibition.

**2. The Bag of Rules**
   * **Metaphor:** We all carry a "big bag of rules" — personal, cultural, and religious conditioning. The *content* of the bag differs (e.g., personal diets, religious doctrines), but the *act of carrying the bag* is universal human suffering.
   * **Lesson:** Spiritual work is about **lightening this bag**. The ultimate goal is to carry only one essential "rule": "If it causes *dukkha*, let it go" (*Dukkha, Dukkha, Nirodha*). This connects to the Wiccan motto cited: "Do what you will, just don't cause harm."

**3. The Diet / Doughnut Rule**
   * **Story/Example:** Making a rule like "I'm on a diet" sets up failure and frustration. It's a form of unskillful renunciation.
   * **Lesson:** The skillful approach is **moment-to-moment investigation**: "Is *this* doughnut, *right now*, a wise choice for my well-being?" This emphasizes present-moment choice over long-term, rigid plans.

**4. The Sword of Destiny**
   * **Metaphor:** "He who lives by the sword dies by the sword." Habitual thoughts and actions forge our "destiny" or character. If you habitually wield aggression (the sword), that pattern will determine your fate.
   * **Lesson:** You can **change your destiny by changing your thoughts** in the present moment. This leads to the punchline: There's no "free will" for those enslaved by habits, but there is **"expensive will"**—the costly, effortful practice of retraining the mind to regain autonomy.

**5. The Door to Paradise**
   * **Metaphor:** The door to internal delight/paradise is **right here, right now**. We often wander out (into distraction) or lock ourselves in a prison of rules. The practice (the Eightfold Method) is the key to open the door and step back into freedom whenever we wish.
   * **Lesson:** Happiness is not a distant destination but an always-available state accessed through present-moment awareness and release of burdens.

**6. The Orchestra Tuning**
   * **Metaphor:** Life can be like an orchestra warming up—a cacophony of individual noises (duality, disagreement, personal rules). Practice is like **tuning** to the same note (A), creating harmony (non-duality, unity, "at-one-ment").
   * **Lesson:** We can find inner peace (harmony) by letting go of the need to judge things as "good/evil" or fight with other "instruments," and instead tune into a state of acceptance and unity with the present reality.

**7. The Submarine in an Ocean of Unity**
   * **Metaphor:** We are like a submarine in an **ocean of unity** (paradise, interconnectedness). Our sense of separation (duality) is like desperately trying to keep the water out. The leak of "I, me, mine" floods us with suffering.
   * **Lesson:** The peace we seek is already all around us; the problem is our effort to separate ourselves from it through selfish wanting and judgment.

**8. Pizza / Food Cooling (for Nibbana)**
   * **Metaphor:** **Nibbana (Nirvana)** is like taking pizza out of the oven. You must let it **cool** (*nibbana* literally means "to extinguish" or "cool") before you can enjoy it without getting burned.
   * **Lesson:** Nibbana isn't a mystical afterlife state but a **present-moment experience of "cooling"**—the mind relaxing, letting go of the "heat" of craving, aversion, and delusion.

**9. Enlightenment as "Lightening Up"**
   * **Wordplay Metaphor:** **Enlightenment** has two practical meanings: 1) Shedding **light** on the truth of your experience, and 2) **Lightening** your load (dropping the bag of rules).
   * **Lesson:** It demystifies enlightenment as a non-magical process of clear seeing and releasing burdens.

**10. The Three P's (Permission, Power, Protection)**
    * **Framework/Story:** A psychological model from the 70s used as a teaching story:
        * **Permission:** You don't need external approval to be happy.
        * **Power:** You have the innate ability to choose happiness.
        * **Protection:** Choosing happiness won't cause catastrophe; you are "protected" in that state.
    * **Lesson:** Addresses the hidden rule ("I don't deserve happiness") and empowers direct responsibility for one's inner state.

### **Overall Narrative Theme**
The talk weaves these metaphors into a coherent story: We are **burdened by a self-created prison of rules** (bag, diet, sword destiny, locked door). The path out is not through more rigid rules, but through a **moment-to-method of mindful investigation** (checking the phone, the doughnut, the thought). This practice allows us to **open the door to the paradise that is already here**, tune into harmony, cool the mind, and lighten our load. The central enemy is **duality** (good/evil, me/other, rules/freedom), and the goal is **unity, ease, and coolness** in the present moment.

results.text: Speaker A: Arya hasn't shown back up. He cut himself off, but he hadn't joined the call yet again. He'll call in a minute. So welcome to the Sunday services. We are all here to worship nothing, the great big grand glorious nothing. And the best part about worshipping nothing is that you don't have to care. There's no care, no worries, no problems. In fact, DJ just asked me a question about the word care, and the first place that we need to go is to define the word and what it means, because the word has more than one meaning. And I think that it did, and in fact you continued to use the word while you slipped in a new meaning for it and carried on from there. You made a left turn without putting out your arm for a left turn signal. Okay, so let's go for care by going to the issue of freedom, because freedom is different than caring, that in fact in some cases is exactly opposite. But there are two kinds of freedoms that we have in the world, and two uses for the word freedom. One is the freedom to, and the other one is the freedom from. Now, the freedom to means— in fact, freedom to is wrong view, that things are cheap, they're free, I can go get what I want and I'm not going to cause any repercussions. And an extreme example of that in the time of the Buddha is the guy who can go to the Ganges this side and kill 500 cattle and then swim across the river and kill 500 cattle on the other side, and he will suffer no damage because the Kamma machine does not exist. Kamma won't affect him. Okay, the reality though is that if you start killing some guy's cows all the guys in the neighborhood are going to be there, I don't think he can get 500 killed. I think maybe 20 is his limit without an AK-47 or something. And so, the possibility of the absurd is recognizing that Kamma is not some magical machine in the sky, but it is actual wake or the damage that we do, it's our weight that when we swing around, we do damage with it. So, freedom too is dangerous, because it's actually giving ourselves permission to full steam ahead, damn the torpedoes. Which works in a movie. But the point is that there is also the freedom from, and the freedom from is, let us say, the full steam ahead, or it's freedom from. So here's an example: you've got a young teenage boy who wants to go to town, and he wants to borrow the keys for the car from his dad, and he wants to have the freedom to drive the car and go where he wants and do what he wants to do. His brother is sitting there on the couch because he is free from the desire to go take the car someplace. You get the distinction? One of us is trapped by our freedom-to, and the other one is free because he's free from that trap of the freedom-to. So we can now look at the word care, because the care has the same sort of barbs with it. And you use the word about with it— care about. And there's another word that we can use that changes the definition slightly, and that's the word care for. And that changes the whole use of the word and the meaning of it. Care about and care for. So we can care about money, but there's not much caring for it. I mean, even investing in the stock market is still caring about it. So we can see it now in the sense of either ownership and control, in the sense of caring about that. I care about my daughter, therefore she'd better do what I tell her to do. As opposed to care for her, which is nourishing her. So this is actually— this kind of caring then goes very well into the understanding that Freud had about the superego state that was carried on with Eric Berne when he changed the name from the superego into the parent. Looking at, in fact, that there's two kinds of parenting: the parents who care about their kids, and then the ones who care for their kids. These are the two kinds of ways of caring, and that what I have been inviting all of you guys to do— hello, Timmy, glad to see you back— so The parenting then has two styles: the style of caring about, which means ordering about, and then the child is going to learn a whole lot of rules, because this is where all— in fact, this is the silabatic paramasa, is the caring about. And the caring for then is the nurturing. So you have two kinds of parenting: you have critical parents And you have nurturing parents, and each one of us had two individual parents, most of us had, but anyway, we were parented by something, we got here. You're an adult now, you made it, congratulations, you're alive, you were parented well enough to make it here, and that parenting was a mixture of critical parenting and nourishing parenting, or the caring for, versus the caring about. And each individual parent will move back and forth between those two things ignorantly, without knowing what they're doing. And in fact, it almost always starts off in nurturing parent when the child is a very tender infant. And in fact, an example of that is the new puppy that we've got. We got a 6-year-old puppy, and I've been letting her bite my fingers and all kinds of stuff. But last night she went too far. And because she went too far, now times are beginning to change. I'm beginning to start teaching her. For instance, I've decided to not— because I've actually lost a hard drive before with a puppy, I've decided not to let this puppy under my feet where there's a hard drive or two. That's my working station. So Now, instead of just picking her up, I've actually yelled at her, told her no, slapped her face, and picked her up and pushed her out. Because now it's time for her to learn the word no. Okay, so this is an example now that I've actually intentionally changed from the nurturing parent into the critical parent. You got to give them a little bit of rules. If you don't— if you give a child 100% nurturing parent, which happens sometimes, you'll wind up with a Caligula or something. There, when a child learns no boundary, then he will see it as freedom to do anything he wants.

### Summary

This Dhamma talk, led by Dhammarato (Speaker A) with Sangha friends, revolves around the nuanced meaning of the word **"care"** and how understanding its two dimensions is central to Buddhist practice and a happier life.

Here is a summary of the key points:

### **Core Distinction: "Care About" vs. "Care For"**
The entire talk explores the critical difference between two types of care:
*   **"Care About":** This is linked to control, ownership, rules, and ideals. It's a conditional, critical, and often fearful form of care focused on outcomes and preservation. It leads to clinging, suffering (dukkha), and a mindset of "freedom **to**" get what one wants.
*   **"Care For":** This is linked to nurturing, nourishment, and unconditional support. It's a gentle, accepting, and compassionate form of care focused on well-being in the present moment. It leads to comfort, satisfaction, and a mindset of "freedom **from**" desires and traps.

### **Key Analogies and Explanations**
1.  **Two Freedoms:** The talk begins by distinguishing "freedom to" (indulging desires, often ignorantly) from "freedom from" (being free from the trap of those desires). The latter is the true aim.
2.  **Parenting Styles:** The two types of care are compared to parenting styles:
    *   **Critical Parent:** Represents "caring about." It sets rules and boundaries, necessary for survival but potentially leading to neurosis if overdone.
    *   **Nurturing Parent:** Represents "caring for." It provides safety, comfort, and love.
    A healthy upbringing (and a healthy mind) needs a balance, but most people err toward the critical, rule-based side.
3.  **The Sutta Example:** The story from the Sutta (SN 3.25, "Grief Comes from Those Who Are Dear") illustrates that grief arises from *clinging* to loved ones ("caring about"). If one "cares for" them, one can love them while accepting the inevitable nature of change and loss, thus avoiding paralyzing grief.
4.  **The Puppy Analogy:** Dhammarato uses his new puppy to show the practical shift from pure nurturing (allowing biting) to introducing necessary rules ("no" to protect hard drives). This demonstrates the need for skillful balance.

### **Application to Dharma Practice**
*   **The Path:** The Buddha's path, when done correctly, should be "good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end." If practice feels difficult and joyless, it's a sign one is likely operating from a place of "caring about" (striving, self-criticism) rather than "caring for" (nurturing, gentle attention).
*   **Anapanasati (Mindfulness of Breathing):** The practice is reframed as an act of **"caring for" oneself**. By bringing a nurturing, wholesome attention to the breath and body, we cultivate wholesome feelings and comfort *right now*, rather than striving for a distant goal.
*   **Self-Relationship:** We must learn to soften the internal "critical parent" (the superego) and start nurturing the inner "child" (the part that feels emotions—both painful and pleasant). This internal shift from criticism to nurture is the essence of the practice.
*   **Honesty & Investigation:** "Caring for" oneself allows for honest self-assessment and correction without the shame or denial that comes from a rule-based ("caring about") mindset. It aligns with the Kalama Sutta's injunction to investigate and know for oneself, not just believe.

### **Additional Discussions**
*   **Four Types of Paths:** The group briefly discusses the sutta (AN 4.162) describing paths that are fast/slow and painful/pleasant. They conclude that a "slow and easy" path, focused on nurturing ("caring for") and skill development, is ideal. Difficulty arises from passionate/critical striving ("caring about") and a lack of developed spiritual faculties.
*   **Understanding Delusion (Moha):** In response to a question, Dhammarato explains that delusion is essentially believing something to be true without investigation. The antidote is to catch oneself using the word "believe" and to instead investigate present-moment reality. He also offers a four-quadrant model (win-win, win-lose, lose-win, lose-lose) to characterize wise, criminal, helpless, and "stupid" (deluded) mindsets.

### **Conclusion**
The talk is a practical guide to reframing one's entire approach to life and meditation. By shifting from a mindset of **"caring about"** (which is rooted in fear, control, and future/past preoccupation) to one of **"caring for"** (which is rooted in present-moment nurture and acceptance), we make the Dharma a source of immediate well-being and ease. The ultimate goal is to cultivate a wise, nurturing inner environment that leads to freedom.

### Metaphors and Stories

Based on the transcript, the speaker uses several **metaphors and stories** to illustrate the core teachings about "caring about" vs. "caring for" and the nature of freedom and delusion. Here’s a breakdown:

---

### **1. Metaphors**

**A. Freedom "To" vs. Freedom "From"**
- **Metaphor of the teenage boy and the car keys**:  
  - One brother wants the **freedom *to*** drive the car (trapped by desire).  
  - The other brother has the **freedom *from*** that desire (content on the couch).  
  - Illustrates how "freedom to" can be a trap, while "freedom from" is true liberation.

**B. Parenting Styles as a Metaphor for Mental Habits**
- **Critical Parent vs. Nurturing Parent**:  
  - Drawn from Eric Berne’s Transactional Analysis.  
  - **Caring *about*** = controlling, rule-based, critical (like a critical parent).  
  - **Caring *for*** = nourishing, supportive, nurturing (like a nurturing parent).  
  - Used to show how we often treat ourselves with critical, rule-based thinking instead of kindness.

**C. The Puppy Training Metaphor**
- The speaker’s new puppy is allowed to bite playfully at first (nurturing), but when it goes too far, he sets boundaries (critical).  
- Illustrates the **need for balance** between nurture and rules—too much nurture creates chaos (a “Caligula”), too much control creates neurosis.

**D. The Four Quadrants of Human Behavior**
- A **2x2 matrix** used to explain delusion, greed, and anger:  
  1. **Wise (Win-Win)**: Cares for self and others.  
  2. **Criminal (Win-Lose)**: Angry/exploitative.  
  3. **Helpless/Helpful (Lose-Win)**: Pleasure-seeking but self-sacrificing.  
  4. **Stupid (Lose-Lose)**: Deluded, harmful to self and others.  
- This maps the “three poisons” (greed, hatred, delusion) onto social outcomes.

**E. The "Stumping Your Toe in the Dark" Metaphor**
- Getting up at night without turning on the light because you *think* you know the way—then stubbing your toe.  
- Illustrates **delusion**: acting on assumed knowledge without checking present-moment reality.

---

### **2. Stories**

**A. The Buddha’s Time: The Cow Killer**
- A man believes he can kill cattle on both sides of the Ganges without karmic consequences because “Kamma is not a magical machine.”  
- Used to criticize the idea of **“freedom to” without responsibility**, and to explain Kamma as the natural “wake or damage” we create.

**B. The Sutta: "Grief Comes from Those Who Are Dear" (SN 3.8 or AN 5.49)**
- A layman hears the Buddha’s teaching and debates it with gamblers. A servant girl hears it, takes it to Queen Mallikā, and through inquiry becomes a *Sotāpanna*.  
- The **story of the dying son** is highlighted:  
  - **Caring *about***: Rushing him to the hospital in a panic.  
  - **Caring *for***: Holding him peacefully as he dies.  
- Teaches that attachment (“caring about”) leads to grief, while loving without clinging (“caring for”) brings peace.

**C. The Kindergarten Lesson Story**
- References the essay *“All I Really Need to Know I Learned in Kindergarten.”*  
- Rules like “put away toys,” “stand in line,” “listen” are foundational—they start as external rules but can evolve into wise, internalized virtue.  
- Connects to how **precepts** begin as rules but can become nurturing guides.

**D. Musashi the Samurai**
- The legendary swordsman Miyamoto Musashi, who used a broken sword in battle and later retired to a cave for enlightenment.  
- Illustrates how **skills developed in worldly life** (focus, presence, discipline) can accelerate the spiritual path if redirected wisely.

**E. The Martial Arts Anecdote**
- The speaker’s experience with a black belt whose arm felt “like a brick” due to conditioned tension.  
- Teaches the importance of **skillful, timely application** of strength—and by extension, the need to apply Dharma skills at the right moment.

---

### **3. Recurring Analogies**

- **Driving & Turn Signals**: Making a “left turn without signaling” symbolizes shifting definitions without clarity.  
- **Web of Lies**: Lying about a lie creates a tangled “web”—shows how rule-based morality (“thou shalt not lie”) can lead to more dishonesty, while nurturing honesty allows correction.  
- **Stock Market vs. Nurturance**: “Caring about” money is like investing for control; “caring for” is like nourishing growth.

---

### **Summary of Core Teaching Through Metaphor/Story**
The speaker uses these examples to contrast:
- **Caring *about*** = control, attachment, suffering, “freedom to,” critical parent, delusion.
- **Caring *for*** = nurture, acceptance, peace, “freedom from,” nurturing parent, wisdom.

The path is framed as moving from the former to the latter—both in how we treat others and, crucially, how we treat ourselves in meditation and daily life.

results.text: We can actually change our attitude in this moment, out of the attitude of a victim, into the attitude of, "Never mind, start again." 'Let me take a deep breath and relax.' And if we keep doing that over and over and over again, we begin to get the idea that, 'Hey, we can do this, we can become successful at it. It is possible that I can learn to control my mind.' This, by the way, I'm introducing as the fourth element on the Eightfold Noble Path. The fourth element is called Samma Sanghappa, and it has a whole lot to do with confidence. You've got to build up the confidence. The Pali word, by the way, is Shraddha or Saddha, the ability to know that I can do this, I can change my attitude, I can change my thoughts. Now, Ivan, you were asking this question before, And the question that you were asking actually comes from the victim's position of, "Oh, I can't change this until I know why it happened." And the answer is, you don't need to know why, you just make the change. You don't have to go victimize yourself saying, "Oh, well, I need help, I need solutions, I need answers, and then I'll change." We can just make the change. That's an important aspect of the way that we practice. Now, here's the point about that, is that by being a victim, we've got no free will. We've got to do what we were told to do. That in fact, the telling of us of what to do, is actually our destiny. You got to do it this way, you got to do it that way, and if you keep doing it the same way over and over again, that becomes kind of a destiny. And then, being a victim, we blame destiny on some higher power. We said God did it, God set my destiny, I can't change it, I've got no free will. There's many things that you can find in our language that supports that. Have you ever heard of the phrase, 'He who lives by the sword dies by the sword'? Isn't that a point of destiny? It also has a lot of reality. You can imagine that the swordsman at the age of 20 is very good with that sword. He's been practicing it for years. And he'll whack anything. He'll whack steak, he'll whack a sapling, he'll whack a banana tree, he'll whack bamboo. And now if you get in his way, he'll whack you. But if he continues to use that sword at 25, and then 30, and then 50, and now at 75 he's still using that sword Guess what? He's going to slow down and somebody's going to whack him. He who lives by the sword eventually is going to get whacked with one. Sometime or another, we've got to make a change and put down that sword. So, looking at the fact that we have habits, we can change the habits, that the habits are what defines our destiny. Here's a little point: the thoughts that you have lead to the feelings, the feelings that you have lead to your speech, the speech that you have leads to your actions, the actions that you have lead to your habits, and the habits you have lead to your destiny. Thoughts, feelings, speech, action, habits, destiny. Each one of them takes longer and longer. Your thoughts are very quick, your feelings are a little slower, your speech is coming in. Then we have behavior, and the behavior over and over again will lead to habits, and the habits lead then to our destiny. So where is the easy place to change our destiny? Is it to change our habits? Or maybe to change our actions? Or maybe to change our speech? Or maybe to change the way that we feel? Or maybe the easiest way to do it is start by changing our thoughts. Those are the easy things to change. And so, if we begin to change our thoughts moment by moment, we can begin to change our attitude, we can change our feelings, we can change the way that we think, the speech, we can change our actions, we can in fact change our habits. And when we really change our habits, we can actually change our destiny. Now, the question about free will is that do you have free will, or do you in fact have no will at all? And they see it as a kind of black and white: you're either run by your habits and run by your destiny, or maybe somebody, some big God or some Kamma machine or some sky daddy or whatever, he's the one that sets your destiny. The reality is that our habits set our destiny. Our habits set our destiny. So, if you start making those little changes, one after another, after another, you can begin to change your destiny. But that doesn't make it free will, and in fact, the whole point is that nothing is free, until you are free. And I'll use the word 'free' in the sense of freedom is just another word for nothing left to lose. You got to lose your habits, you got to lose your actions, you got to lose your speech, you got to lose your feelings, and you got to start thinking in a way that is ways to get rid of this stuff. All of these old bad habits only fall away once you start making some changes in your actions, and the easiest way to change your actions is to stop your bad habits, to stop your bad action. Another way of looking at it is, in order for you to stop your bad behavior and your bad actions, is to shut your mouth, to shut up. Don't talk yourself into being angry. And the way that we shut our mouths is by stop feeling bad. And the way that we can stop feeling bad is by changing our thoughts, which is the easy way into it. So, the answer to that is, is that there is no such thing as a free will, But there is such a thing as will, it's just expensive. It's going to cost you. You're going to have to make those changes, and if you keep making those changes over and over again, you can begin to have will. And the more will that you have, and the more you exercise it, the better it gets. And the more you stop running your mouth, the more you stop behaving badly, the more you stop having those bad habits, then you come down to not having much of anything at all, and that's where real freedom comes in. Freedom is just another word for no more bad habits. You've got nothing left to lose.

### Summary

Based on the Dhamma talk, here is a summary of the key points:

**Core Question:** The talk began with a practitioner (Ivan) asking about the skillful way to deal with unwholesome feelings. He questioned the common advice to "just let it go," feeling that this sometimes leads to the feelings returning more strongly. He wondered if he needed to "digest" or investigate the feelings first.

**Dhammarato's Core Teaching:** The central answer is that the Buddha's path is a **"change model," not an investigative or contemplative model.** The goal is not to analyze where a negative feeling came from (its "origin story"), but to recognize it is present and *immediately* make a skillful change.

**Key Principles Explained:**

1.  **Right View & Mindfulness (Sati):** Right View is not a fixed ideology (like conservative vs. liberal). It is the **verb of looking**—waking up (*"wakey wakey"*) to see what is happening in the present moment without getting lost in stories about the past or future. This is true *Sati* (often mistranslated as mindfulness).

2.  **The Problem with Investigating Origins:** Dwelling on "why" a bad feeling arose keeps you stuck in the story and in the role of a **victim**. It's compared to being startled by a monk who entered quietly and wasting time asking "Where did you come from?" instead of simply acknowledging "Hello, you are here." The past is one of the "Four Imponderables"; the present is where work can be done.

3.  **The Framework for Change - The Four Aspects:** We operate in four interconnected domains:
    *   **Body:** The most stable (e.g., posture, comfort).
    *   **Feelings/Emotions:** More fluid (e.g., anxiety, joy).
    *   **Mind State/Attitude:** Can change in minutes (e.g., victim, winner, confident).
    *   **Thoughts:** The fastest, changing by the second.
    These all condition each other. A tense body leads to anxious feelings, which lead to negative thoughts, and vice-versa.

4.  **The Practical Method - Change Your Thoughts:** The **easiest point of intervention** is at the level of thoughts. We habitually "talk ourselves into" bad feelings. We can consciously "talk ourselves into" good, **wholesome, and true thoughts**.
    *   **Examples:** "Everything is okay right now." "I am safe." "I can handle this." "I am successful." "I can relax."
    *   This requires **Right Effort**. It is not "toxic positivity" (lying to yourself), but choosing to focus on true, wholesome aspects of your present reality (e.g., "There is no snake in my room right now. I am physically safe.").

5.  **Building Confidence and Changing Destiny:** By repeatedly making these small, successful changes in thought, you build **confidence** (*Saddhā*). This changes your attitude from victim to someone capable and "wealthy" in Dhamma. This process alters your feelings, speech, actions, and ultimately your habits and destiny. **Free will is not free**—it is earned through this repeated, effortful practice of making skillful choices, culminating in a freedom where you have "nothing left to lose" (no defilements).

6.  **The Role of Environment:** Practice is best done in **seclusion and safety** (like the Buddha's instruction to go to the forest). If your environment is truly dangerous, leave. If it's safe, your wholesome thoughts about safety can be genuine and effective.

**Dialogue & Skepticism:** The talk included a skeptic (Mike) who resisted this as "manipulation" and "toxic positivity," preferring a method of passive observation until fascination with negative thoughts fades. Dhammarato responded that there is **no guarantee** passive observation leads to change; it often perpetuates habit. He advocated for **active, wise effort** to change now, rather than waiting for desperation to force a harder change later (like dieting only after a health crisis).

**Conclusion:** The skillful way to deal with an unwholesome feeling is:
1.  **Wake up** to its presence (*Sati*).
2.  **Do not** invest in the story of where it came from.
3.  **Immediately** apply Right Effort to change your **thoughts** to wholesome, truthful ones relevant to the present moment.
4.  This will shift your mind-state, feelings, and eventually your entire being toward peace and freedom.

The talk emphasized that this approach, framed within the **Eightfold Noble Path** and practiced through exercises like **Ānāpānasati** (mindfulness of breathing), is a practical discipline for ending suffering here and now.

### Metaphors and Stories

Based on the talk, the speaker (Dhammarato) uses several **metaphors and stories** to illustrate the Dhamma (Dharma) and correct practice. Here are the key ones:

### **Metaphors**
1.  **The Monk Who "Flew" into the Room:** This is the central metaphor for the mistake of over-investigating the origin of unwholesome feelings. The story of a monk (or the speaker himself) quietly entering a room and startling someone illustrates that asking "Where did this come from?" is irrelevant. The point is to recognize what is present *now* ("Here he is") and deal with it, rather than getting lost in stories about its origin.
2.  **The Felled Tree:** Used to explain the importance of an upright attitude (and posture). A tree falls in the direction it leans. Similarly, if our mental attitude "leans" toward being a victim or a certain worldview, we will fall into corresponding thoughts and habits. The practice is to cultivate an "upright" attitude that doesn't lean, ensuring stability and comfort.
3.  **The Swordsman ("He who lives by the sword..."):** This metaphor explains how habits create destiny. A swordsman who practices his skill for decades will eventually be defeated by it when he slows down. Our habitual thoughts and actions similarly shape our future. To change destiny, we must change our habits, starting with our thoughts.
4.  **The Four Elements (Earth, Water, Fire, Wind/Smoke):** A metaphorical framework for the four foundations of mindfulness (Satipatṭhāna):
    *   **Body = Earth:** Stable, changes slowly.
    *   **Feelings = Water:** Fluid, changing.
    *   **Mind States/Attitudes = Fire:** Can change quickly, energizing or consuming.
    *   **Thoughts/Mind Objects = Smoke in the Wind:** The fastest-moving and most ephemeral.
5.  **"A Stitch in Time Saves Nine":** Used to emphasize the "change model" of practice. Instead of contemplating a problem (like examining nine bad stitches), it's better to correct it immediately (unravel and re-stitch) when you first notice it.
6.  **"Freedom is just another word for nothing left to lose":** A re-framing of the famous lyric to describe the goal. True freedom (or "free will") is not the ability to do anything without consequence, but the state of having lost all defilements, bad habits, and cravings—there's "nothing left to lose," leading to contentment and kindness.
7.  **The Diet:** Used to counter the idea that change happens automatically when we get tired of old patterns. Just as someone must consciously decide to diet to avoid health consequences, we must consciously decide to change our thoughts, not wait for a desperate crisis to force change.

### **Stories & Anecdotes**
1.  **The Victimhood of Human Infants:** A story about human development to explain our default attitude. Unlike animals that can walk soon after birth, humans are born completely dependent ("victims"). This victim attitude is reinforced by parents, school, and society, and we carry it into adulthood, looking for external saviors (like religions). The practice is to shift from this innate "victim" attitude to an "I can do this" attitude.
2.  **The Man at the Refrigerator:** A short anecdote to summarize the core teaching. A man meditating finds himself at the open fridge, wondering how he got there. The lesson is not to trace the steps (the origin) but to wake up to the present reality ("I'm at the fridge") and make the skillful change ("close the door and go back to sit down").
3.  **Political Examples (Democrats/Conservatives, Rich/Poor):** Used not as political commentary but as analogies for "ordinary right view" and "wrong view." They illustrate the conventional world's belief in cause-and-effect, rules, and consequences, which the Buddha's "right view" transcends by focusing on direct observation without fixed conclusions.

### **Core Conceptual Metaphors**
*   **Practice as a "Change Model," not a "Contemplation Model":** The entire talk contrasts two approaches: digging into the past to find roots vs. immediately changing present unwholesome states.
*   **Thoughts → Feelings → Speech → Actions → Habits → Destiny:** This is presented as a causal chain. The easiest place to intervene and change destiny is at the beginning: by changing our thoughts.
*   **"Free Will is Expensive":** Will is not inherently free; it must be built through effortful practice. What we call "free will" is actually the **result** of that practice—a state of freedom *from* defilements, not freedom *to* do anything.

In summary, the speaker uses vivid, everyday metaphors and relatable stories to move the discussion away from abstract "meditation" and toward a practical, effort-based "Dhamma" of immediate observation and change.
